property_summary: For any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract C only accepts calls to its fallback when msg.value == 10 ether (so the call completes and updates pastBlockTime), whereas the mutant that requires 5 ether will accept a different set of msg.value — thus the universal rule: after calling fallback with an arbitrary value, reference C's fallback call succeeds iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant accepts instead when msg.value == 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed values that make the reference revert but the mutant succeed (or vice versa).

For any caller and any msg.value, calling C's fallback succeeds (does not revert) if and only if msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant requires 5 ether instead, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs where the reference reverts but the mutant does not (and vice versa).

For every call to C's fallback with arbitrary msg.value and caller, the reference contract succeeds (does not revert) iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant instead requires 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value values for which the reference reverts but the mutant does not (or vice versa).

For any caller and any sent ether amount, calling C's payable fallback succeeds (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant instead accepts msg.value == 5 ether, so some fuzzed msg.value make the reference revert while the mutant succeeds.

For any caller and any sent ether amount, calling C's payable fallback succeeds (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant requiring 5 ether breaks this rule for some msg.value so there exist inputs where the reference reverts but the mutant does not (or vice versa).

Reference C only updates pastBlockTime when the call's block.timestamp is strictly greater than the previous pastBlockTime (i.e., time must increase); the mutant removes that check allowing pastBlockTime to be set even when timestamp does not advance, which can make pastBlockTime remain equal to block.timestamp across repeated calls in the same timestamp.

For any caller and block timestamp, calling fallback with exactly 10 ether on contract C never leaves pastBlockTime equal to a strictly older timestamp when block.timestamp has advanced (i.e., the reference only updates pastBlockTime when timestamp increases), whereas the mutant can set pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp even when time did not advance and thereby allow pastBlockTime to be overwritten so that two sequential calls in the same block can make pastBlockTime remain equal to block.timestamp contrary to the intended monotonic update rule.

For the correct contract C, calling fallback with exactly 10 ether never updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp has not advanced (i.e., pastBlockTime only increases when timestamp strictly increases); the mutant removes that time-order check and thus can update pastBlockTime even when timestamp stays the same, causing a difference observable via the public getter.

For all calls with msg.value == 10 ether, the reference C only updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp strictly increases (so two sequential successful fallback calls made in the same block will leave pastBlockTime unchanged after the second call), whereas the mutant updates pastBlockTime even when timestamp does not advance — so there exists a sequence of two calls in the same block where the mutant's pastBlockTime equals the current block.timestamp but the reference's pastBlockTime does not change on the second call.

For the reference contract C, calling its payable fallback with exactly 10 ether never changes pastBlockTime when block.timestamp does not increase (i.e., pastBlockTime only updates on calls made at strictly later timestamps); the mutant removes that check and therefore can update pastBlockTime even when timestamp stays the same, breaking this monotonic-time-update property.

For any caller and timestamp, when calling fallback with exactly 10 ether the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the (strictly) recent block.timestamp and then returns successfully; the mutant that assigns pastBlockTime before checking can cause the require(block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) to fail (revert) for some inputs, so the mutant can revert while the reference never does.

For any caller and any block.timestamp, calling fallback with exactly 10 ether on the reference contract always succeeds (does not revert) and sets pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp; the mutant that sets pastBlockTime before checking can cause a revert (failing call) for some combinations of timestamp/ordering, so the mutant may make the low-level call revert while the reference never does.

For any caller and any block.timestamp, calling fallback with exactly 10 ether on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) and leaves c.pastBlockTime equal to the current block.timestamp; the mutant that updates pastBlockTime before checking can cause the call to revert for some timestamps/ordering, breaking this universal success property.

After any successful call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract only transfers its balance back to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance == 0 iff block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant inverts the condition and thus for some block numbers the balance observation differs.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether at a strictly increasing timestamp, the reference contract either keeps its balance (when block.number % 15 != 0) or drains it to the caller (when block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant inverts the conditional so for some block numbers the post-call contract balance differs from the reference.

For any call to fallback with exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp increases, the reference contract forwards its entire balance to the caller whenever block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance becomes 0), whereas the mutant that calls transfer(0) does not forward the balance and thus address(c).balance remains > 0 for some inputs.
